name: Searchfit AI
tagline: Tracks and tries to improve how a brand shows up in AI search answers instead of classic blue links.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The mechanic here is not mysterious: ask a bunch of models a bunch of buyer-intent questions on a schedule, see whether your brand gets named, log it, chart it. An agent can build that loop in a weekend, and for a single brand with twenty prompts it will be good enough to tell you whether you are invisible. What you cannot cheaply build is breadth: many models, many locales, repeated sampling to beat answer variance, and months of history to prove a change did anything. The other half of these tools is the advice layer, the part that tells you which pages and schema to fix, and that is a consultant in a trench coat either way. Build it if you want one dashboard for one brand; pay if you need the longitudinal record.
coreLoopDIY: Runs a saved list of prompts against a few LLM APIs on a schedule, detects whether your brand and competitors get mentioned or cited, and stores every run so you can chart share of voice over time.
requirements: API keys for at least two model providers, ideally ones with live web search enabled
A budget for tokens: sampling the same prompt repeatedly is the whole point and it costs money
A machine or small VPS that can run a daily cron job
A real prompt list, which is the actual work and nobody can generate it for you
whatYouLose: Coverage across many models, regions and answer modes, which is where most of the subscription price goes
Months of baseline history you did not start collecting, so your first chart is a flat line
Competitor benchmarks drawn from other customers' tracked prompts
Citation-source analysis that tells you which pages the models actually pulled from
The recommendation layer, such as it is, plus the reporting PDF your client expects
moatNotes: The defensible asset is the time series, not the scraper. Every day you did not run it is a day you cannot backfill.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because agencies need a chart with twelve months on the x-axis, and because running the same query a hundred times across five models with web search on is a real infrastructure and token bill that is genuinely cheaper to rent. Also because AI search visibility is currently a panic purchase: people buy a dashboard to prove they are doing something about it, and a self-hosted script does not come with a logo to put on the slide.
notes: The scraper is a weekend; the history is not. Start logging today even if you never build the pretty part.
prompt:
Build a local AI search visibility tracker. Single Node 20 + TypeScript project, no framework, no cloud account, no telemetry.

Stack, non negotiable:
- TypeScript, run with tsx, no bundler
- SQLite via better-sqlite3 for all storage, file at ./data/visibility.db
- Model calls to OpenAI and Anthropic APIs via plain fetch, keys from .env (OPENAI_API_KEY, ANTHROPIC_API_KEY)
- Report output as a single static HTML file with inline CSS and one inline chart drawn as SVG, no JS libraries

Config: a config.yaml with brand name, brand aliases, brand domain, a list of competitor names, and a list of prompt strings grouped by intent tag.

Core loop, implemented as `npm run track`:
- For every prompt, for every configured model, send the prompt N times (default 3, configurable) and store each raw answer text, model id, timestamp and run id
- Detect mentions: case insensitive match of brand name and aliases, plus competitor names, plus any URL containing the brand domain
- Record per answer: mentioned yes/no, first-mention character offset, cited domain list extracted from URLs in the answer
- Compute per prompt and per run: mention rate, average position rank among all detected brands, competitor mention rates
- Store everything, never overwrite, every run is append only

`npm run report` reads the DB and writes ./out/report.html: current mention rate per prompt, share of voice vs competitors, a time series of overall mention rate per run date, and the top cited domains across all answers.

Also include `npm run export` dumping all runs to CSV.

In scope: the sampling loop, the SQLite schema with migrations as plain SQL files, retry with exponential backoff on 429, a cost estimate printed after each run, an example config.yaml with 15 realistic prompts.

Out of scope: user accounts, a web server, auth, scheduling UI, recommendation engine, anything that writes to a third party service. For scheduling just print the crontab line to add.

Write a README that says plainly: the value of this tool is the accumulated history, so run it daily starting now, and do not change the prompt list casually because it breaks comparability.
